title: What is AWS Kinesis Data Analytics — a managed service for processing and analyzing streaming data in real-time using SQL or Apache Flink, without managing infrastructure — and what is its relationship to Apache Flink (uses Flink as the underlying engine)?
shortTitle: What is AWS Kinesis Data Analytics and its relationship to Apache Flink

s1_definition.profdef: AWS Kinesis Data Analytics, now branded Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink, is a fully managed service for processing and analyzing streaming data in real time without provisioning or operating servers. It runs your stream-processing logic, authored either as Apache Flink applications in Java, Scala, Python, or SQL, or historically as standalone SQL, and it handles cluster provisioning, scaling, patching, checkpointing to durable storage, and high availability for you. Its relationship to Apache Flink is direct: the service uses Apache Flink as the underlying execution engine, so a Flink application you write runs on a managed Flink runtime, giving you Flink's full capabilities, event-time processing, state, exactly-once, without you having to run the cluster.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India wants the power of a Flink streaming engine to analyze transactions in real time, but it does not want to hire a team to install, patch, scale, and babysit a Flink cluster. Kinesis Data Analytics is like leasing a fully staffed, always-running processing facility: the bank brings its recipe, the Flink application, and the facility operator handles the building, the staff, the power, the backups, and scaling up during busy season. The bank still writes the same Flink logic it would run itself, but it never touches a server, because the managed service runs Flink underneath on its behalf.
s1_definition.oneliner: Kinesis Data Analytics, now Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink, runs your Flink or SQL streaming applications on a fully managed Flink engine, handling provisioning, scaling, checkpointing, and availability so you never operate the cluster yourself.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** AWS Kinesis Data Analytics, now branded Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink, is a fully managed service for processing and analyzing streaming data in real time without provisioning or operating servers. It runs your stream-processing logic, authored either as Apache Flink applications in Java, Scala, Python, or SQL, or historically as standalone SQL, and it handles cluster provisioning, scaling, patching, checkpointing to durable storage, and high availability for you. Its relationship to Apache Flink is direct: the service uses Apache Flink as the underlying execution engine, so a Flink application you write runs on a managed Flink runtime, giving you Flink's full capabilities, event-time processing, state, exactly-once, without you having to run the cluster.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India wants the power of a Flink streaming engine to analyze transactions in real time, but it does not want to hire a team to install, patch, scale, and babysit a Flink cluster. Kinesis Data Analytics is like leasing a fully staffed, always-running processing facility: the bank brings its recipe, the Flink application, and the facility operator handles the building, the staff, the power, the backups, and scaling up during busy season. The bank still writes the same Flink logic it would run itself, but it never touches a server, because the managed service runs Flink underneath on its behalf.

**One line to remember:** Kinesis Data Analytics, now Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink, runs your Flink or SQL streaming applications on a fully managed Flink engine, handling provisioning, scaling, checkpointing, and availability so you never operate the cluster yourself.

sections.s2_technical:
The service exists because running production Flink yourself means operating a JobManager and TaskManagers, sizing memory, configuring state backends and checkpoint storage, handling upgrades, and building high availability, which is substantial operational work. Kinesis Data Analytics removes that by offering a managed Flink runtime. You package your Flink application, for example a jar built against the Apache Flink DataStream or Table API, and deploy it to the service; AWS provisions the underlying Flink cluster, runs your job, and manages its lifecycle. The service's capacity is expressed in Kinesis Processing Units, each roughly a bundle of compute, memory, and networking, and you can enable automatic scaling so the number of units grows and shrinks with load. State is checkpointed and snapshotted to durable AWS storage automatically, and the service maintains high availability and restarts your application on failure, preserving exactly-once where your sources and sinks support it.

Because the engine is genuinely Apache Flink, you get Flink's programming model unchanged: event-time windows, watermarks, keyed state with RocksDB, timers, the DataStream API, the Table API, Flink SQL, and connectors. The natural sources and sinks are the AWS streaming and storage services, Kinesis Data Streams, Amazon MSK for Kafka, S3, DynamoDB, OpenSearch, and others, which the service integrates smoothly, including identity and access management for secure access and CloudWatch for metrics and logs. There are two main flavors historically: the Apache Flink applications flavor, where you write real Flink code and it is the strategic, fully-featured option, and an older SQL-only flavor that let you write streaming SQL over Kinesis streams without Flink code, which was simpler but far more limited and is the legacy path. The modern recommendation, reflected in the rename to Managed Service for Apache Flink, is to build Flink applications.

The senior nuances are these. First, the service is Flink, so skills and code are portable: an application developed for open-source Flink runs on the managed service with minimal change, and you can move off if needed, which limits lock-in at the application layer even though the operational conveniences are AWS-specific. First, you still own the application logic, including correct watermarking, state time-to-live, and choosing exactly-once with compatible sinks; the service manages infrastructure, not correctness of your business logic. Second, scaling is by Kinesis Processing Units with optional autoscaling, and you tune parallelism and units to throughput and state size just as you would size a self-managed cluster. Third, you trade some control, you cannot freely tweak every Flink configuration or install arbitrary cluster-level components, for a large reduction in operational burden. Fourth, cost is pay-per-use on the units consumed, so right-sizing and autoscaling matter for the bill. Understanding that the service is a managed wrapper around real Apache Flink, so you keep Flink's full model while offloading operations, and knowing where your responsibility ends and AWS's begins, is exactly what distinguishes an engineer who has deployed streaming in the cloud from one who only knows open-source Flink.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India wants real-time fraud scoring on its transaction stream using Flink's event-time windows and keyed state, but it has no appetite to staff a team to run and patch a Flink cluster around the clock. This is exactly what Kinesis Data Analytics provides: the same Flink application running on a managed Flink engine.

Problem 2 — Transaction volume spikes massively on salary days and festivals, so the processing capacity must scale up automatically and shrink afterward to control cost. This is exactly the Kinesis Processing Unit autoscaling the managed service offers.

In the mini-project we build a runnable demo that models the relationship between a Flink application and the managed service, and the autoscaling behavior, without touching AWS. We define a `FlinkApplication` representing the portable Flink job logic, a `ManagedFlinkService` that hosts the application, provisions Kinesis Processing Units, checkpoints automatically, autoscales units with load, and restarts on failure, and a throughput feed that rises and falls. A `KdaDemo` main class deploys the application to the managed service, pushes varying load, and prints how units scale, how checkpoints are taken, and how a simulated failure is recovered, all while the application logic itself is unchanged Flink code.

The service configuration this demo models:

```properties
# app.properties — Managed Service for Apache Flink application config
application.name=fraud-scoring
runtime=FLINK-1_18
flink.parallelism=8
kpu.autoscaling.enabled=true
kpu.min=2
kpu.max=32
checkpoint.enabled=true
checkpoint.interval.ms=60000
source=kinesis:transactions
sink=kinesis:fraud-scores
```

Java source files:
sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run the demo
java -cp target/kda-managed-flink-service-1.0.0.jar com.bank.kda.KdaDemo

# Real deployment via AWS CLI:
aws kinesisanalyticsv2 create-application \
  --application-name fraud-scoring \
  --runtime-environment FLINK-1_18 \
  --service-execution-role arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/KdaRole
```
sections.s5_journey:
The input is a fraud-scoring Flink application, a managed service configured for two to thirty-two Kinesis Processing Units, and a load profile that rises on salary day then subsides.

Step 1. The Flink application is deployed to the managed service. The service provisions the minimum two units and starts running the application. The point is that the application is ordinary Flink code; the service simply hosts it.

Step 2. Normal load of one thousand five hundred records per second arrives. At roughly one thousand records per second per unit, the service needs two units, which it already has, so no scaling happens. The service then takes an automatic checkpoint to durable storage, recording the records processed since the last checkpoint. The bank wrote no checkpointing code; the service does it.

Step 3. A salary-day spike of twenty thousand records per second arrives. The service computes that about twenty units are needed and autoscales from two to twenty units to keep up, staying within the thirty-two maximum. It then takes another automatic checkpoint. This elastic scaling is the managed benefit.

Step 4. A sample transaction for SAV2001 of nine hundred thousand is scored by the application logic, returning a score. This confirms that the same Flink business logic runs unchanged under the service while AWS handles the operations around it.

Step 5. A failure occurs. The managed service restarts the application from the last checkpoint automatically, with no operator intervention, preserving the processed state. The bank did not build any recovery machinery.

Step 6. Load subsides to three thousand records per second. The service autoscales down to the units needed for that load, reducing cost. The final unit count reflects the lower load. The journey shows the core idea: the application is portable Flink code, and the managed service provisions, checkpoints, scales, and recovers around it.

Final output:

```

2024-01-01 00:00:00 INFO    auto-checkpoint at 60000 (records since last=1500)

2024-01-01 00:00:00 INFO    auto-checkpoint at 120000 (records since last=20000)

```

sections.s6_takeaway:
AWS Kinesis Data Analytics, now branded Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink, is a fully managed service for processing and analyzing streaming data in real time without provisioning or operating any servers. I package my stream-processing logic, authored as an Apache Flink application in Java, Scala, Python, or SQL, and deploy it to the service, and AWS provisions the underlying Flink cluster, runs the job, and manages its whole lifecycle, including scaling, patching, automatic checkpointing to durable storage, and high availability with automatic restart on failure. Its relationship to Apache Flink is direct and important: the service uses genuine Apache Flink as the underlying execution engine, so I keep Flink's full programming model, event-time windows, watermarks, keyed state with RocksDB, timers, the DataStream and Table APIs, and Flink SQL, while offloading all the operational burden.

The value is removing operations without sacrificing capability. Running production Flink myself means operating a JobManager and TaskManagers, sizing memory, configuring state backends and checkpoint storage, handling upgrades, and building high availability, which is substantial work. The managed service does all of that, expressing capacity in Kinesis Processing Units that can autoscale with load, checkpointing automatically, and integrating cleanly with AWS sources and sinks like Kinesis Data Streams, Amazon MSK, S3, DynamoDB, and OpenSearch, with IAM for security and CloudWatch for metrics and logs. The senior points I always make are that because the engine is real Flink, my code and skills are portable and lock-in is limited at the application layer even though the operational conveniences are AWS-specific; that I still own correctness, meaning watermarking, state time-to-live, and choosing exactly-once with compatible sinks, while AWS owns the infrastructure; that scaling is by Kinesis Processing Units with optional autoscaling so I right-size for throughput, state, and cost; and that I trade some low-level configuration control for a large reduction in operational toil.

At the National Bank of India we wanted Flink-grade real-time fraud scoring on the transaction stream but had no desire to staff a round-the-clock cluster-operations team. We wrote the fraud-scoring job as an ordinary Flink application with event-time windows and keyed state and deployed it to the managed service, which ran it on a managed Flink engine, checkpointed it automatically to durable storage, and kept it highly available. On salary days and festivals, when transaction volume spiked many times over, the service autoscaled the processing units up to keep latency low and then scaled back down afterward to control the bill, all without any code change, and when the application once failed, the service restarted it from the last checkpoint automatically with no operator intervention. Being able to explain that the service is a managed wrapper around real Apache Flink, so I keep Flink's full model while AWS handles provisioning, scaling, checkpointing, and recovery, and to draw the line between my responsibility for business-logic correctness and AWS's for infrastructure, is exactly what shows I have run streaming workloads in the cloud rather than only on a laptop.
